a1-pronouns-copula.title: Pronouns & the Verb "To Be"
a1-pronouns-copula.pattern: ӕз дӕн (I am) · ды дӕ (you are) · уый у (he/she/it is) · мах стӕм (we are) · сымах стут (you all are) · уыдон сты (they are)
a1-pronouns-copula.explanation: Unlike its Northeast Caucasian neighbors (Chechen, Avar), where "to be" changes shape to agree with the grammatical class of its SUBJECT NOUN, Ossetian's copula conjugates by PERSON, much like Russian or English "to be": ӕз (I) takes дӕн, ды (you) takes дӕ, уый (he/she/it) takes у, мах (we) takes стӕм, сымах (you-plural) takes стут, and уыдон (they) takes сты.
a1-pronouns-copula.fact: The 3rd-person singular has a second, less common form, ис, alongside у -- academic sources treat these as having a subtle distinction (existential vs. predicative), which is genuinely nuanced enough that this course only teaches у for now rather than risk blurring the two together incorrectly.

a2-present-full.title: Present Tense: Full Conjugation
a2-present-full.explanation: Now that you know the "you"-form (-ыс), here's the complete present-tense pattern for regular verbs, using дзурын ("to speak") as the model: дзурын (I speak -- identical in form to the infinitive itself), дзурыс (you speak), дзуры (he/she/it speaks), дзурӕм (we speak), дзурут (you all speak), дзурынц (they speak).
a2-present-full.fact: The 1st-person-singular present is spelled exactly like the infinitive (дзурын means both "to speak" and "I speak") -- context and the subject pronoun are what tell them apart, not the verb form itself. Every one of these six endings is independently attested in natural sentences, not derived by a single blanket rule.

a2-present-2sg-negation.title: Present Tense (You): -ыс & Negation: нӕй
a2-present-2sg-negation.explanation: Regular verbs form the "you" (singular) present tense by dropping the infinitive ending -ын and adding -ыс: дзурын (to speak) -> дзурыс (you speak), хӕрын (to eat) -> хӕрыс (you eat). To negate the copula in the present tense, Ossetian uses the special fused form нӕй ("is not") rather than combining нӕ with у.
a2-present-2sg-negation.fact: нӕй isn't simply нӕ ("not") plus у glued together -- it's its own fused negative form, which is why it looks different from what you might expect. This course only teaches the "you"-form of regular verbs and the 3rd-person negative copula for now; the rest of the person/tense paradigm needs more confirmation before being taught.
